I had a lively discussion with my uncle earlier today about whether or not journalists and reviewers should disclose if they have donated to a Kickstarter or Patreon campaign. My uncle is nominally a GamerGate supporter and believes in what GamerGate stands for, but isn't very active in online communities.

My uncle argued that in most cases a journalist shouldn't have to disclose if they donated to the Kickstarter or Patreon of a product or person that they are covering, because the journalist receives no financial gain from the donation (only the recipient does).

He argued that there are some exceptions to this, such as if they are a major donor (i.e. thousands of dollars) to the project/person, thus representing a potential conflict of interest. My uncle also argued that it places a large burden on journalists to keep track of every single donation they have ever made, which could be an extraordinarily long list after many years. He argues it could lead to situations where journalists are being cited for ethical violations for donations they made decades ago and have long since forgotten about. With that being said, he fully supports journalists disclosing when if they receive donations from Kickstarter or Patreon.

I argued that they should disclose their donations to projects or people that they cover, as it is still a financial tie. I also argued that often-times there are special rewards that backers receive and that oftentimes when people donate to a cause, they feel psychologically invested in it and want to see it succeed. In addition, I argued that as a journalist, it is their job to do everything they can to ensure they are performing their job in a professional and ethical manner.

There is also the possibility that journalists donating to content creators is indeed a quid-pro-quo in some cases, either intentionally or unintentionally. Often times the people (journalists and developers) in question are very cliquish and have ties with each other, which is why they are donating in the first place. My uncle countered this by stating that such a line of thinking is presuming the guilt of the journalists, rather than assuming that they are innocent until proven guilty.

I do think there are some situations where journalists would need to donate to a Kickstarter or Patreon campaign in order to gain early access to a product, thus allowing them to cover the product in question. I do not believe this is inherently unethical and is merely part of a journalist doing their job. I do think my uncle raises a few interesting questions for discussion.

  • Should journalists disclose one-way donations they make to projects/people, if they are receiving nothing in return?

  • If so, should they always disclose such donations or only when they exceed the amount required to gain access to the product?

  • If not, is there a certain amount of money where you would think it would be necessary (i.e. an extraordinarily large donation)? What if they receive a backer perk as part of their donation?

  • Does treating all journalist-to-developer donations as potential conflicts of interest create a situation where journalists are perceived as guilty until proven innocent?
[Discussion] Journalists donating to Kickstarter and Patreon campaigns

My uncle also argued that it places a large burden on journalists to keep track of every single donation they have ever made, which could be an extraordinarily long list after many years. He argues it could lead to situations where journalists are being cited for ethical violations for donations they made decades ago and have long since forgotten about.

I don't think anyone would blame a journalist for donating to a project then writing about another one a decade later, not realising that one of the sound guys worked on both of them. This is more a situation where journalists are very much active fans and supporters of a particular person or group, then use their position to cover their projects. Not that I'd expect all games journalists to purely cover stuff they're ambivalent towards, but donating to someone's kickstarter or patreon is a step beyond that. Also, part of the reason GG objected so strenuously is because those relationships didn't exist in a vaccum, they were another strand in the web of cliquedom which has surrounded online games journalism. If it were just a case of someone donating to a stranger's kickstarter then covering it I doubt anyone would have blinked an eye, but they were also personal friends, lovers and housemates with their subjects.

If I were a journalist, I'd disclose whatever amount I donated beyond what was required for access to the game, because who does it hurt?

However, we might be able to tell something is fishy if Nathan Grayson says he donated $1,000 to Depression Quest and then mentions it out of 50 other games.

There is also the possibility that journalists donating to content creators is indeed a quid-pro-quo in some cases, either intentionally or unintentionally. Often times the people (journalists and developers) in question are very cliquish and have ties with each other, which is why they are donating in the first place. My uncle countered this by stating that such a line of thinking is presuming the guilt of the journalists, rather than assuming that they are innocent until proven guilty.

I do think there are some situations where journalists would need to donate to a Kickstarter or Patreon campaign in order to gain early access to a product, thus allowing them to cover the product in question. I do not believe this is inherently unethical and is merely part of a journalist doing their job. I do think my uncle raises a few interesting questions for discussion.

  • Should journalists disclose one-way donations they make to projects/people, if they are receiving nothing in return?

  • If so, should they always disclose such donations or only when they exceed the amount required to gain access to the product?

  • If not, is there a certain amount of money where you would think it would be necessary (i.e. an extraordinarily large donation)? What if they receive a backer perk as part of their donation?

  • Does treating all journalist-to-developer donations as potential conflicts of interest create a situation where journalists are perceived as guilty until proven innocent?
[Discussion] Journalists donating to Kickstarter and Patreon campaigns

Well, ask your uncle this:

Should a journalist disclose that they donated to a presidential candidate that they are covering on the campaign trail? Can they be trusted to cover them fairly? Is it fair to say that it would color a reader's interpretation of a journalist's coverage if they knew of the journalist's donation? How is this any different than your discussion above?

The wedding is in 3 weeks, and we've been engaged for 3 months (yeah, we know it's short). We've been dating for 1 year and 3 months, and have been friends for 3 years.

We've been arguing a lot lately, to the point that it's effecting our excitement about marriage. I'm getting cold feet now, and yesterday she told me she is too.

To make things even more complicated, she's pregnant (unplanned pregnancy, but we both want to keep the baby. This is a different story). I think her being pregnant brings a sense of obligation for us to get married also.

But I think our lack of excitement could be a result of the stress of planning a wedding and the changes in life it will bring. I've heard of people getting scared before marriage, only to feel glad the still went through with it afterwards. I can't tell if that's our situation, or if we are just doing this because of the baby. Yes, we were engaged before we knew she was pregnant.

You know that feeling of "I built my bed, now I have to lay in it?" I think there's some of that going on. But it doesn't mean we don't love each other. We've shared some amazing life experiences and our connection has grown pretty deep.

But then again... a few weeks ago when I announced to one of my friends that I was getting married, he recognized right away that I didn't sound very excited and inquired as to why. I didn't have a straight answer for him, since I don't even know myself. But he was right - I don't get excited when I talk about it.

Also, we've been arguing a lot lately. It has finally subsided, but the arguments have not helped at all.

Here's the thing, there's also a lot of stress in our lives right now, so I'm trying to determine if the lack of excitement is a result of the stress, or if I'm really not wanting to get married. The wedding is only 3 weeks away!

Here's a few stressful things we have going on, to list a few:

  • She's pregnant. It was a surprise, and we found out just after we got engaged. This brings multiple factors:
  • - 1. She's going through night sickness daily and hormonal shifts, of which makes her cranky and that stuff.
  • - 2. We haven't told anybody because we don't want this fact to distract from our wedding - aka we are not getting married because she is pregnant, but our family might think so. Therefore we're waiting until after the wedding to announce the little one.
  • Our engagement is a short one - 3 months - so planning a wedding this fast has been insane. We are keeping things simple though, and that helps. But still, weddings require a LOT of planning.
  • We still have to find a place to live. We don't share an apartment right now and finding one to move into has been difficult (we've been looking for 2 months). Not to mention expensive and time consuming. Sometimes I think this would help the most if we already had a living space figured out.
  • We've been arguing a lot lately. I took a 2 week work trip and got home 2 weeks ago - but she was livid that I was gone that long before our wedding and wanted me here to help. The trip was NOT a vacation - it was to do major repairs on a rental property I own, and that was the only window of time I had people to help me with it. I made arrangements for us to coordinate wedding plans over Skype and a shared google doc, but she just fought with me the whole time I was up there and nothing got done.

Also, yesterday she told me that she's not feeling happy. After talking about it we discovered that she is still angry with me for taking that 2 week trip (Reminds me of the stories married men tell where the woman remembers something that happened years ago, and won't forgive). I talked to her in the best way I could, and apologized, and thanked her for opening up to me. That conversation actually helped a lot and today she seems much more peaceful about the situation.

Still, I wonder if this is just a bad mix of life-stress and pregnancy combined. OR, is my gut trying to tell me we're not ready for this? How normal is it to get cold feet before marriage?

tl;dr: Getting married in 3 weeks and we keep arguing with each other. Now I'm getting cold feet. A short engagement and a pregnancy is not helping either.

The happiest marriages usually have the smallest weddings. The planning and the economic cost is a real drag on a relationship. Its just a useless ceremony that doesnt need to cost that much. If you really like each other you dont need a bravado of a wedding to prove it.

Just my 2 cents

I'd say get married in court with close friends and family as witnesses. Figure out the living situation and baby shit. Put off the wedding ceremony until you guys are less stressed and feel more in control of your lives. Good luck and congrats! Hope you both feel better :)
I definitely agree. Other than hanging some lights, and nice table cloths with a center piece, we're not doing much as far as decorating. But even the small things start to add up.
Yeah, but it's kind of late for them to change anything TBH.

Life is stressful, you need to be able to support each other through it and you will come out stronger in the end.

As for the trip you took, it seems a bit lengthy was it something you'd been planning for a while? Maybe she saw it as you trying to escape the stress and leaving her behind to cope. Make sure she knows you're there for her and help with the wedding planning whenever you can, if you look excited for it she'll feel more comfortable and hopefully be in a better mood :) Getting cold feet is normal.

Wish you all the best, you can do this! Support support support each other!

Is the wedding what you're arguing about for the most part? Then it's more likely wedding stress. If it's feasible try to scale back the wedding a little. And (even if scaling back isn't feasible) you two should take a day to yourselves to remember why your getting married. Go on a nice simple date somewhere, and then go back to one of your places and just spend some time together! Don't talk about the wedding, don't talk about finding a place. You can talk about the baby if you can keep it lighthearted and excited (baby names and pink toesies), but don't talk about your birthing plan or saving for college. Reminiscing is always a good option.

Just be your normal selves to each other for a while, pretend like there is no wedding, remember that you love each other, and (wedding or not) you both love each other and spend your lives together.

If you don't already you should try to schedule regular proper dates, and some alone time wherever you can fit it in your schedule. You don't need your conversational rules to be as strict as this first one, but a 'keep it lighthearted' ruled isn't a terrible idea if you've been arguing a lot lately.

You don't make the decision to skydive on the plane, you make it at the ariport. You're already on the plane the only thing to do is jump.

Who knows, maybe you'll enjoy it.

Honestly it sounds like the whole situation is stressing both of you out beyond words. Getting married is supposed to be something that is done with joy and excitement. If instead it is causing division and stress, maybe now is not the time. Could you imagine yourself having a conversation like this with her?

  • I love you
  • I want to be with you and with our baby
  • I want to marry you
  • Planning this specific wedding at this specific time is stressing us both out and damaging our relationship
  • Maybe we should postpone it until after the baby is born?
  • I love you
  • I want to be with you and with our baby

Thanks for your responses everyone. From what I gather, stress is stress, and this is no reason to back out. There has been a sense of isolation which needs to be addressed, but this is not a reason to back out. I know nothing's perfect, but it's good enough to keep fighting for. The wedding will continue as planned.
